title: Slave and emperor
hookLine: Epictetus enslaved, Marcus on the throne: one school, very different lives

cards: Two men. One was born into slavery, in a town in what's now Turkey: owned, sent where he was told, and, tradition says, walking with a limp.
The other was born generations later into a wealthy Roman family, marked out young for the throne, and became emperor of Rome. Two lives could hardly be further apart.
And yet the emperor learned how to live from the slave's words.

teach.b: The first man is Epictetus. Even his name carries his story: in Greek it means acquired, the kind of word you'd use for property.
His owner, Epaphroditus, served at the court of Nero, and at some point the young man heard the lectures of Musonius Rufus, yesterday's teacher. Later he was freed.
He taught in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, then opened a school in Nicopolis in Greece.
He didn't write his teachings down himself: a student named Arrian did, and that's the Discourses and the Handbook this path keeps quoting.

The second man is Marcus Aurelius. At the start of his Meditations he thanks the people who formed him, among them his tutor Rusticus, for introducing him to the discourses of Epictetus and lending him his own copy.

So the emperor learned freedom from the notes of a former slave. And they teach the same thing: what's up to us is our own judgment and choice, and nothing else. Epictetus pictures it in his Handbook.
You're an actor in a play, and the author gives out the parts: maybe a poor man, maybe a ruler, maybe someone who's lame.

teach.h: PLAY THE PART YOU'RE GIVEN WELL.
teach.b: Your job is to play the part well; choosing it isn't yours. From a man handed slavery, that's not a slogan. To a man handed an empire, it's a warning not to confuse the costume with the person.
One school, two very different parts, the same work.

how: Readers of Stoicism often study Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius side by side, and reflect on playing well the role life has handed them.

games.q: Epictetus says life is like a play. you've been handed a part you'd never pick. what's your job?
games.why: in the Handbook the author gives out the parts; our work is to play ours well, since choosing it isn't ours.

practice: Think about the part you were handed, not chosen: the family, the body, the place and time you were born, the money or lack of it. Notice it without judging whether it's fair.
Then ask quietly: within this part, what's mine to play well today?

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, born into slavery, whose words the emperor Marcus Aurelius later learned from: one school, very different lives, the same teaching.

orig.note: Greek: acquired, gained; the name of the enslaved philosopher.

carryVoice: Your line: the same school. Rich or poor, enslaved or crowned, the work is the same. That's day two hundred ninety-six.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.9.29 (Epictetus and Musonius); Arrian's preface to the Discourses
